meaningMnemonic: You know the animal radical. This is just like that with a little extra. It's an animal already... which means all you have to do is remember what kind of animal. In this case, it's a badger .
Stand up on the moon so you can look down on your countries. The thing with all the lines and borders are the borders of all the countries you rule, for you are an imperial .
You're sliding some dirt around with a tree you cut down. This contraption you've made is called a plow . Use it to push dirt around!

Imperial clothes allow you to perform an ancient attack that cannot be repelled. Hints IMPERIAL ATTACK, GO! Imagine what this imperial attack might look like and imagine yourself in some swanky imperial clothes while you perform it.
readingMnemonic: The attack 's power is concentrated in the shoe s ( しゅう ) in this imperial outfit. You attack with your feet, kicking the enemy with your old, fancy shoes. Hints Picture the shoes as you attack, they glow—full of attack power! These +4 attack shoes are really special.

meaningMnemonic: If you stick some flowers to your right lapel and bare your heart to someone, you'll be sure to attract them. Hints It's important that the flowers be on the right — otherwise, they might block all the attractive energy pouring out of your heart (which is hopefully on your left).
readingMnemonic: Whenever you attract someone, you feel a certain hea t ( ひ ) in the air. That heat is the first sign of the fiery passion that's about to erupt between you and this person you've attracted. Hints You're really heating up the room with all the attraction you're generating in here.

meaningMnemonic: A good moon is a bright moon. Not just in terms of light, but in mood as well. Like, gee wiz, what a bright, happy moon. Hints Picture the good, good bright moon. Shining and shimmering and smiling down at us on Earth.
readingMnemonic: It's so bright that you can see all the roe ( ろう ) in the sea glowing and reflecting the light like stars. And the tiny baby fishies inside the roe are smiling brightly back up at the moon! Hints Picture this scene like it's a Disney cartoon. The good moon is smiling brightly down at the roe which are smiling right back. They might even start singing a song!

meaningMnemonic: Below the canopy of tree s is a hand . The hand is just there to chafe against the trees. Hints There's a hand just chafing against some trees. That's... interesting.
readingMnemonic: As the hand chafe s on the trees, it says ma ma ( ま ), mama. Hints This is the hand of a child looking for its mama. And, it chafes against trees to try and find the warm, soft touch of its mama. Instead, it only finds rough bark, so it continues its chafing.

meaningMnemonic: You have to run , put your ear on the stool , then run back. That's the charm of this game. Hints Imagine yourself playing this game and basking in the charm of tapping your ear on the stool.
readingMnemonic: The added charm of this game is that there's this big chu te ( しゅ ) at the end. It's so charming because you love chutes. Hints As you watch, you really see the charm of this game. Some people are throwing the stool down the chute, some people are sliding down it on their ears...how charming.

meaningMnemonic: The loiter ing mountain king who hangs around during winter to provide an indication (this kanji uses the "indication" kanji as its top 2/3rds) of things to come now looks into your heart , and only sees bad things. So, he chastise s you about it. Hints "What's in your heart is no good," he chastises you.
readingMnemonic: Why is he chastising you, really, though? He foretold Mrs. Chou coming back in a previous mnemonic, but you saved Mrs. Chou on the beach (once again, in a previous mnemonic), so you could have prevented her second coming. He is chastis ing you for saving Mrs. Chou ( ちょう ). Hints In the 潮 kanji you saved Mrs. Chou from dying, so he is chastising you for it.

meaningMnemonic: We put up a flag to remember where we tried to use a jackhammer to take a measurement of your friend's heart . Granted, it was a terrible idea, but hopefully that flag of remembrance is some kind of consolation ? Hints Obviously it's not good enough consolation. Be furious about this.
readingMnemonic: Even though you weren't happy with the flag, you were even more frustrated to watch an ea gle ( い ) swoop down and grab the flag and fly away with it. Hints Now you have absolutely nothing. Not even a consolation flag.

meaningMnemonic: A badger , at the root of its heart , is a courteous creature. Hints They may seem gruff and rude at first, but they'll still let you in their home in the middle of winter unannounced and offer you tea, a warm fire, and a place to sleep.
readingMnemonic: Badgers are especially courteous to con dors ( こん ). Condors live in the trees while badgers live in burrows under those trees. When humans tear down the condor's homes, the badgers who live below them always let them stay over until they get back on their feet. Hints Picture a courteous badger taking care of an injured, and now homeless, condor. It's fluffing the condor's pillows, bringing it soup, and patting it on the shoulder saying, "There, there."

meaningMnemonic: The sun hits this and breaks into three sun s. What can split the sun in three directions? A crystal ! Hints Crystals take light and refract it around into many directions. That's why there are three suns in this kanji.
readingMnemonic: Who is hoarding and harnessing the power of these crystal s? That would be the Shou gun ( しょう ). Hints Imagine the Shougun lying in his bed of crystals. He still has his really serious, angry face though. Even as he rubs the crystals to his face, he's glowering.

meaningMnemonic: A bamboo stalk looks the same as a big ol' cylinder . Hints Compare the two things in your mind and make them the same.
readingMnemonic: Picture a cylinder shaped とう きょう . All the buildings are cylinders. The city itself is cylinder shaped too. Even... gasp! The people of とうきょう ! Hints とうきょう is a really weird city now that they passed the cylinder law. Imagine it so deeply that it weirds you out.

meaningMnemonic: You're struck by a tsunami , mauled by a canine , and then set on fire . It seems the universe is trying to destroy you. Hints A tsunami, a canine attack, and a fire disaster make for quite a triple-whammy. What'd you do to make the universe want to destroy you so badly?
readingMnemonic: Actually, the universe wants to destroy you because you're a Mets ( めつ ) fan. The universe despises the Mets — why do you think they haven't won a World Series since 1986? Hints Imagine pulling on your Mets jersey only to suddenly receive a tsunami warning on your phone. Then, you hear a canine growling and catch a whiff of something burning nearby. Uh-oh, the universe is trying to destroy you again!

meaningMnemonic: A canine and a woman stand before you, radiating dignity and might . Who is this majestic pair? Hints Try to imagine who this woman might be. A world leader? A powerful CEO? Whatever the case, she's got an aura of dignity — and that giant canine behind her only makes her look even more mighty.
readingMnemonic: Just when you thought this woman couldn't emit any more dignity , an ea gle ( い ) swoops down and perches on her shoulder. The huge canine behind her already gave her a dignified aura, but this eagle has made her look positively awe-inspiring. Hints Imagine trying to crack a joke in front of this mighty woman, only to be silenced by the dignified stare of her eagle. You just can't make lighthearted banter with someone who's got an eagle on their shoulder.

meaningMnemonic: A foot on a giant is a pretty long distance for a normal person to walk. Giants have big feet and can travel large distance s very quickly. Hints Compare the distance you can travel with one step compared to a giant. It's a considerable difference in distance.
readingMnemonic: Going to Little Kyo to ( きょ ) is a short distance for a giant but a long distance for you. Hints Imagine walking the distance between where you are and the (possibly made up) Little Kyoto. Think about the distance.

meaningMnemonic: If the rain touches your foot and gives it a little rain kiss , you know that part of your foot is expose d to the elements. You can also see some dew forming on your exposed foot. So that's what rain kisses are! Hints Ugh, you shouldn't have bought these open toed shoes, at least not during rainy season!
readingMnemonic: You run along the ro ad ( ろ ), trying to get out of the rain, but the road keeps going and going, with walls on both sides. Hints You wonder how long this road will go. With exposed toes, your feet are going to get all wet with dew if you can't get off this blasted road.

meaningMnemonic: A fire door is a door that leads to something full of fire. That thing is a furnace . Hints Open the fire door and feel the heat of the furnace . Hot!
readingMnemonic: You're using the furnace to melt tar to put on the ro ad ( ろ ). Hints Smell the tar baking from the furnace. Feel the heat from the furnace. Fix the road, while you're at it.

meaningMnemonic: You've been ordered to spear this tree but you decide to be really gentle instead. Hints Imagine gently poking the tree with your spear. You glance around nervously, hoping no one notices how easy on it you're being.
readingMnemonic: You're being really gentle to the tree when a jewel ( じゅう ) falls out of its branches and hits you on the head. Hints The jewel has a little note on it, "Thank you for being gentle." Did... did the tree just reward you for being gentle?!

meaningMnemonic: Two king s are here right now ! We need to entertain them otherwise who knows what they'll do. Get out the harp , or the zither , or something. Hints Imagine yourself playing a harp or a zither, even if you don't know how. Entertain these kings to the best of your ability, right now. That's why you're doing it and not someone who knows what they're doing. They want it now.
readingMnemonic: You may already know that a Japanese harp is called a こと , but here's a mnemonic to help you if you don't: When playing your harp , you always wear your coat ( こと ). Hints Your harp playing is pretty bad, so you put your coat on just in case you need to leave in a hurry to escape an angry audience.

meaningMnemonic: Look at the dirt on the ground at dawn and you'll be able to see all the hedge s growing in the area really well. At any other time of day, hedges tend to blend into their surroundings. But at dawn, the shadows the sun makes really helps them stand out. This hedge also works as a fence . It borders an area and you can't walk through it. A natural fence! Hints Picture yourself leaning over a balcony at dawn, looking at all the hedges appear and their shadows stretch over the ground.
readingMnemonic: You're looking intently at one particular hedge because yesterday you dropped your ca r key s ( かき ) behind it. Now that you know where the hedge is you're going to need to search it to find your car keys. Hints Imagine rooting around under some hedges, desperately trying to find your car keys. Hedges are prickly and there's spiders in here! If only you didn't need a car in the first place!

meaningMnemonic: The root of a stamp is to get an instant picture down. Back in the olden days, people had to make seals and draw out things by hand, so stamps came about so you can—BAM—just stamp it and have what you want in an instant. Hints Lots of things have roots from wanting to have something in an instant. Just think about instant ramen. The root of that was to get ramen real, real fast. Similar to stamps, ya know?
readingMnemonic: Think about the thing you want to make instant . I'd want instant sock s ( そく )! Don't waste time searching for a matching pair or pulling them on. Just take out a pair of instant socks, add water, and the socks are already on your feet. In an instant! Hints Imagine using instant socks. How do they feel? Soggy, but hey, it was fast!

meaningMnemonic: A (fresh water) tsunami . Some horns . The ground . A bunch of poop . Combine these together and let them decompose a while. You'll have yourself some very nourishing soil. Hints The stuff in horns is great for fertilizer. So is poop. So is water (as long as it's fresh water). So nourishing!
readingMnemonic: This is the kind of nourishing soil that Je sus ( じ ) would make if he was into making soil, probably. Hints Imagine him making soil made out of those things. Jesus approves of this nourishing soil.

meaningMnemonic: A cow in the winter doesn't like to leave the barn to go to the pasture . It has to, though, because a cow's gotta eat. Hints It's cold outside (it's winter after all). Imagine you having to herd all the cows out to pasture even though they don't want to leave the warm barn.
readingMnemonic: ぼく is one of the common ways to say "I" in Japanese (which you should remember!). In this case, you're a boy... a cowboy, and you say, " ぼく will take these cows out to pasture !" Hints Actually say that phrase out loud while thinking about bringing your cows to pasture.

meaningMnemonic: The sound of spring water always puts you at peace . Hints Everything from winter is melting and trickling and thawing. All the dripping sounds fill you with a peace you can barely describe.
readingMnemonic: You want to feel this peace all the time, not just in spring, so you dip your tie ( たい ) in the spring water. Now your tie is making the peaceful dripping sounds you love. Hints Imagine carefully dipping all of your ties in the peaceful spring waters and hearing that sweet sound you love at all times.

meaningMnemonic: Take your spoon to the sun to be able to take a bite. It's delicious , you hear. That's the point of the spoon. Hints Taste that delicious sun. It doesn't even burn!
readingMnemonic: This delicious taste is... familiar somehow. You take a few more bites and then scream. It tastes like shee p ( し )! Hints You had your eyes closed because the sun is so bright. When you open them you realize the delicious sun you were eating is really just a giant, really bright, cooked sheep. You should probably point this out to NASA or something.

meaningMnemonic: You take out a flag , lay a towel below it, and use your knife to carve the pattern through them both. Voila! This is exactly how old printing presses used to work. Hints The old way of printing involved taking the pattern you want (the flag), pressing it against the place you want to print it (the towel), then just slicing that sucker on there (with the knife).
readingMnemonic: As you get your flag ready for printing you look over and see Satsu ki ( さつ ), who's already finished a nice pattern on her towel. She's a little young to be using a knife, but her print came out nice. Hints You know her pretty well at this point, so try to imagine what kind of printing Satsuki would make. Picture her holding it up to show you.

meaningMnemonic: The king 's hat , not to mention the hair stuck to said hat, is incredibly rare . If you have your hands on either of these things, you'll be a rich duck. Hints Imagine yourself holding a king's hat covered in his hair. Who will you sell it to? This is such a rare item!
readingMnemonic: Then you look closer at the hat. It's about to get even rare r. Attached to the hair is the king's chin ( ちん ). Hints Not sure how it got there, but you'll make a pretty penny from this. The king only had one chin, so that's about as rare as they come.

meaningMnemonic: People had to use their bamboo plow s long ago to put their name in a register . This is because there was no paper yet, so they would hitch a cow to their bamboo plow, and dig their names into the dirt to create all kinds of registers. Hints School registers, family registers, member registers — you name it. Picture the fields and hillsides back then, full of names scraped into the dirt.
readingMnemonic: If your name is in a register , people will find you very sexy ( せき ). This was true long ago too. There's nothing sexier than someone whose existence is accounted for in official documentation. Hints No wonder people went to the trouble of plowing their names into the dirt back then. They understood the sex appeal of registers.

meaningMnemonic: You use your fingers to hold the roof of the festival up, but it rub s against them. The roof is heavy, and you have to walk to keep up, so the roof is rubbing against them really, really badly. Hints Have you ever been to a Japanese festival? There's always one of those portable shrines that are basically just roofs people hold up. That's what you're trying to hold with your fingers as the whole thing rubs against them.
readingMnemonic: Just when you thought the rub bing couldn't get any worse, Satsu ki ( さつ ) appears and hops up onto the roof. AAGH! It hurts! Hints Picture Satsuki sitting on the roof as you carry it through the festival. She may be a little girl, but her extra weight makes the rubbing so much worse — you can really feel the skin chafing.

meaningMnemonic: You take two clumps of dirt to make a measurement , using them to seal each side of your measuring tape, so it stays on the ground. This is the way people used to seal in things back in the day, back when we didn't have fancy things like tape and glue. Hints Picture sealing other things with dirt. Like the bricks in your wall. Or the hole in your floor. Dirt can seal in anything.
readingMnemonic: You can also seal foo d ( ふう ) in dirt to make it last longer. That's how jerky came about, you know. Seal some meat underground and in a few months you'll have some tasty dried meats to chew. By the way, this has another reading you should probably know. It's ほう . Most sealing is done in the ho me ( ほう ), you know? So just think about eating food in your own home! Hints Dig up your sealed food and eat it in the comfort of your own home. Mm, delicious!

meaningMnemonic: The simultaneous radical and the simultaneous kanji are the same! Hints Know your radicals, yo!
readingMnemonic: What simultaneously protects and kills? Your holy blue sa ber ( せい ). Hints It's also simultaneously here and there at the same time. It moves really fast. And simultaneously glowing blue and white. Your saber is a lot of things all at once!

meaningMnemonic: If a tsunami hits a pirate they are going to sink no matter how good of a pirate captain they are. Hints Tsunamis are big. Pirates are small. Simple as that.
readingMnemonic: As the tsunami comes to sink the pirate, the pirate holds his chin ( ちん ) up high. He will die with dignity. Hints Imagine this dignified chin-holding-up-high pirate. Nod your head, because you know he got what he deserves.

meaningMnemonic: Put your fingers in somebody's business by slap ping them! This method also works if someone is getting too involved in your business. Slaps are basically your way of doing business with your fingers. Hints Imagine giving someone a good, hard slap in the face. You're all up in their business now.
readingMnemonic: ぼく is one way to say "I" in Japanese, usually used by dudes. But you're going to use it now when you slap this guy. Who's in everybody's business, slapping them? ぼく . Hints Say that out loud, using ぼく . You're the boss, the boss of slap business.

meaningMnemonic: When a yakuza takes a knife to clothes , it will of course cause a split or tear . Hints It doesn't matter if it's a yakuza member or not. Any knife will cause a split or tear in clothes.
readingMnemonic: "I want to split and tear that." You agree, so you say Let's ( れつ ) do it. Hints Think of a thing you want to tear with your yakuza buddy. You're into it, so you agree and say "Ret's do it!"

meaningMnemonic: A small tsunami comes in the morning with the moon . That just means the ocean gets bigger when the moon's out, and that my friends is simply the tide . Hints The moon does affect the tides a bit, so you can imagine the tsunami as the water getting bigger whenever the moon is out. That's just the tide.
readingMnemonic: You go check out the tide . The water is coming in a little stronger, and something washes up on the shore. It's a body! You roll the body over and it is Mrs. Chou ( ちょう )! Hints She wakes up and says, "If only you came at low tide then I would never have been saved!" She jumps up and runs off, yelling something about destroying the world.

meaningMnemonic: This construction project made from shellfish will act as a tribute to the Crabigator. Hints The Crabigator is a sea creature (maybe?), so making a tribute from shellfish makes some sense.
readingMnemonic: This great tribute is being commissioned by Emperor こう いち . Hints In his power, こういち has made a new religion around the Crabigator, to put the fear of kanji learning into his subjects. Hint: When you see 工 in a kanji it will often take the こう reading.

meaningMnemonic: A sky attack is an air raid / air attack . Tora tora tora!
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

sentences.japanese: 僕が空を見上げると、ちょうど空襲が始まるところだった。
sentences.english: When I looked up at the sky, the air raid was just about to happen.

meaningMnemonic: You learned another vocabulary word 札 as "amulet," but this is a special honorable amulet . It's a talisman .
readingMnemonic: The reading for the 御 is お because ふだ uses the kun'yomi reading. Kun'yomi + kun'yomi = yes.

sentences.japanese: どうしてここに御札をはっているんですか？
sentences.english: Why did you put the talisman here?

sentences.japanese: これは、地元の神社でもらった御札です。
sentences.english: This is an amulet that I got from the shrine in my hometown.

sentences.japanese: 英語圏の国にも、御札ってあるんですか？
sentences.english: Are there talismans in English-speaking countries, too?

meaningMnemonic: Your sphere might is the force you command over a sphere or ball… in this case, a baseball, making this a pitcher's stuff . If you're not familiar with this baseball term, we recommend giving it a google. In short, it refers to a pitcher's pitches, judged by how inherently hard those pitches are to hit.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

sentences.japanese: 野球のシーズンが到来する春に近づくにつれて、あの投手の球威は益々増しています。
sentences.english: As we get closer to spring and the arrival of baseball season, that pitcher's stuff has been getting stronger and stronger.

meaningMnemonic: If a 原子 is an atom and a 炉 is a furnace , what is a furnace that has atoms? It is an atomic reactor or nuclear reactor .
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

sentences.japanese: 原子炉の建設について、政府に忠告をした人もいました。
sentences.english: Some people warned the government against building nuclear reactors.

meaningMnemonic: An attack attack is an attack or assault .
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

sentences.japanese: 警察の車は、暴走族に襲撃された。
sentences.english: A police car was attacked by a motorcycle gang.

meaningMnemonic: You have rights and might over this area. That gives you authority .
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

sentences.japanese: 権威を失ったのにまだ過去の栄光にしがみついていて、全く往生際が悪いったらありゃしないよ。
sentences.english: He's awfully persistent as he still clings to his faded glory even though he lost his authority.

meaningMnemonic: This may look like a verb at first, but it's actually the adverb version of the adjective 凄い . When something is awful it's usually awfully awful.
readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You've learned this reading already, so you should be able to read this on your own.

sentences.japanese: ベトナムのコーヒー、凄く甘くて驚きました。
sentences.english: Vietnamese coffee was very sweet. I was surprised!

sentences.japanese: 今日は、先生の気分が凄く悪くなったため授業が中止になった。
sentences.english: The teacher's health condition got awfully bad today, so class was canceled.

sentences.japanese: この長靴が凄く欲しいんだけど、Amazon Prime Nowでオーダーする価値あるかな？
sentences.english: I want these rain boots so bad. Do you think ordering them from Amazon Prime Now is worth it?

meaningMnemonic: A 軍艦 is a battleship , and 島 is an island. Welcome to... Battleship Island (go Jurassic Park music).
readingMnemonic: This word uses the on'yomi readings for 軍 and 艦 , and the kun'yomi reading for 島 . You learned all of them, so you should know the reading already! Oh, but watch out for the rendaku.

sentences.japanese: アイツはぜんぜん面白くないな。話題といったら軍艦島の都市伝説だけだし。
sentences.english: He isn’t interesting at all. All he talks about is the urban legend of Battleship Island.

meaningMnemonic: A high furnace is one that's particularly hot and blasty. This is a blast furnace .
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

sentences.japanese: 今朝の朝刊で、その鉄鋼会社は世界一大きな高炉の建設を計画していると読んだよ。
sentences.english: I read in the newspaper this morning that the steel company is planning to build the world’s largest blast furnace.

meaningMnemonic: The decision is split , causing a breakdown in all we've decided. A big ol' rupture . 決裂 is a formal word used when talks or relationships totally fall apart. Since it refers to a full-on rupture and sounds dramatic, you'll often see it in news headlines or news reports when negotiations between companies or countries crash and burn.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

sentences.japanese: 両者の意見が合わず、話し合いは決裂した。
sentences.english: The two sides couldn't agree and the talks broke down.

sentences.japanese: 交渉が決裂した原因は何だと思いますか？
sentences.english: What do you think was the cause of the breakdown in the negotiations?

sentences.japanese: 合意目前での決裂は株式市場に大きな影響を与えました。
sentences.english: The collapse of talks on the verge of an agreement had a significant impact on the stock market.

sentences.japanese: あの男は奴らの決裂を、牢屋の中で舌なめずりをしながら待っていたに違いない。
sentences.english: That man was, no doubt, eagerly awaiting the breakdown of their relationship from within his jail cell.

meaningMnemonic: A bright bright is something that's bright .
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

sentences.japanese: 彼はかつては明朗快活な青年だった。
sentences.english: He used to be a cheerful young man.

meaningMnemonic: This is the na-adjective version of bright . The word is bright or cheerful .
readingMnemonic: Of all the people who are bright and cheerful, one man comes to mind. The cheerful Hulk Hoga n ( ほが ).

sentences.japanese: 朗らかな声をした知らない人から国際電話がかかってきました。
sentences.english: I got an international call from someone I didn’t know with a melodious voice.

meaningMnemonic: Something that you wrap is a bundle or package .
readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You learned it when you learned 包む , but here's a reminder of the mnemonic just in case: Remember how you wrap your bundle s? That's right, with the two two technique. Your package s are always double wrapped.

sentences.japanese: 日付が変わる瞬間に包みを開けてもいい？
sentences.english: Is it okay if I open this package at the stroke of midnight?

meaningMnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well. This word covers a lot of meanings so it can be charm , taste , vibe , or even gist .
readingMnemonic: If something has charm , your thought/ 思 ( おも ) goes in that direction/ 向き ( むき ).  You feel the vibe? Do you get the gist?

sentences.japanese: こんなに趣のあるお持ち帰り用の容器を見たのは初めてです。
sentences.english: I’ve never seen such a tasteful doggie bag before.

meaningMnemonic: Remember how 慰謝 means "consolation?" Add fee to that and you get compensation . Or consolation money , depending on the situation. 慰謝料 refers to compensation for mental or emotional distress. It covers damages for non-physical harm, such as emotional pain in divorce settlements, affairs, or accidents, where the victim seeks financial redress for their distress.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

sentences.japanese: 慰謝料をよこせと脅されています。
sentences.english: They're threatening us to send compensation.

meaningMnemonic: I show my consolation by apologiz ing. This is consolation .
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

sentences.japanese: 保険会社から受け取る慰謝料は、税務署に申告する必要がありますか。

meaningMnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means sink so the verb vocab version is to sink . On a literal level, 沈む refers to physical sinking — a boat sinking into the water or someone's foot sinking into the mud, for example. However, it can also be used metaphorically to talk about things like the sun setting ( 太陽が沈む ), a nation falling into decline ( 国が沈む ), or even someone "sinking" into a depressed mood ( 気分が沈む ).
readingMnemonic: Your boat is about to sink , so you run around yelling, " She's ( しず ) sinking! She's… she's sinking! Abandon ship!" Boats are always female, so be careful not to say "it." If you don't say "she's" sinking, your crew might not get the message.

meaningMnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means split , but if you split something, you are going to tear it or to rip up it.
readingMnemonic: In order to get it open, you need to tear and rip up a sack ( さく ). Sacks don't have tabs or zippers or any of those fancy things. If you want to get at the stuff in a sack you have to tear the top right off!

meaningMnemonic: When you open something seal ed, you're unsealing it or breaking a seal . 開封 generally refers to opening something sealed, like opening a letter or package.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

meaningMnemonic: The " side rope ." This doesn't make much sense. What this is, though (you'll want to look at the reading), is a Yokozuna . This is a Sumo Grand Champion . 横綱 refers to the highest rank in sumo wrestling, because the champion sumo wrestler wears a thick ceremonial rope around their waist. The word can also be used more broadly to describe someone at the very top of their field, like ラーメン界の横綱 (the king of ramen).
readingMnemonic: The readings are the ones you learned with the kanji. Just watch out for the rendaku that makes the 綱 part づな .
